forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Stockport papers cite £5.6bn government funding to cover 90% of council SEND deficits to 2025/26
news_drafts.lead:
A Labour Group amendment before Stockport's Council Meeting on 1 October 2026 calls on government to fund council deficits caused by demand-led services that councils are required by law to provide. It points to what government has already done on one of them: around £5.6bn "to cover 90% of council SEND deficits built up to 2025/26, and a commitment to fund SEND centrally from 2028".

SEND stands for special educational needs and disabilities. Support for it is paid from the high needs part of school funding, the money for children with those needs, and it is one of the council's major cost pressures. The £5.6bn is a national figure covering councils across England. The material does not give Stockport's own share of it, or the size of the council's SEND deficit.

Under the commitment cited in the amendment, government would pay for SEND centrally from 2028 onwards, rather than councils meeting the cost from their own budgets. The material does not record the outcome of the vote on the amendment.
news_drafts.paper_title: Calling on government to fund council deficits caused by statutory demand-led services (Labour Group amendment)

news_drafts.headline: Valuation control weakness from prior audit still unresolved; £11.29m dwellings error found and corrected
news_drafts.lead: Stockport's auditors have found that a control weakness they identified in the previous year's accounts has not been fully addressed. The council's process for reviewing property valuations—checking that internal valuers' reports match the fixed asset register—remains ineffective despite management commitments to improve it. During their 2025-26 audit, external auditors identified a formula error in the dwellings valuation spreadsheet that overstated asset values by £11.29m, a material misstatement that the council corrected before finalising its accounts. The auditors also found a £1.89m overstatement in the Stockport Exchange Holiday Inn valuation, which the council assessed as not material and did not adjust. Separately, internal audit capacity has been cut by 85 days following staffing changes, leaving a 65-day shortfall against revised work plans and forcing deferral of ten audits including high-priority reviews of contract management and anti-fraud work.

findings.headline: Mid-year amendment approved to Minimum Revenue Provision policy to implement IFRS 16 Leases standard, requiring MRP to reflect lease asset value over life of lease rather than just lease liability
findings.detail: Right-of-use assets and lease liabilities brought onto balance sheet 1 April 2024. Mid-year amendment refined MRP treatment to ensure statutory charges amortize the true lease asset value (adjusted for accruals, prepayments, premiums, incentives) over the lease term, not merely the lease liability.
findings.matters: Shows accounting policy refinement in response to mandatory standard change; material to understanding revenue charges for capital-financed leases; peer councils implementing IFRS 16 track policy treatment differences and their revenue impact.
findings.figures: No specific monetary quantum disclosed but policy adjustment will affect MRP charges going forward
findings.quote: MRP charges will be systematically adjusted so that the overall charge over the life of the lease accurately reflects the true value of the right of use asset recognised on transition, rather than just the lease liability.

findings.headline: Combined debt portfolio weighted average rate fell from 3.93% to 3.86%, a 7 basis point improvement, driven by repayment of 5%+ loans and structural shift to cheaper temporary borrowing
findings.detail: General Fund rate declined from 3.82% to 3.70%. HRA rate held steady at 4.53%. Improvement reflects redemption of higher-coupon PWLB tranches (5.32–5.45%) and increased use of temporary borrowing at much lower rates as long-term PWLB rates remained structurally elevated throughout year.
findings.matters: Shows improving debt costs supporting revenue budget headroom; material to lenders assessing debt serviceability and to councils evaluating debt management effectiveness under volatile rate environment.
findings.figures: Portfolio rate 3.93% to 3.86% (7 bps improvement); General Fund 3.82% to 3.70%; HRA 4.53% (unchanged)
findings.quote: The overall combined debt portfolio rate moved down from 3.93% to 3.86% by 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Council investment portfolio achieved exactly 4.10% budgeted return on £35.587m average balance maintained in Money Market Funds throughout volatile year
findings.detail: Return matched budget precisely despite Bank Rate falling from 4.50% to 3.75% during year. Q1 yield 4.39% compressed to 3.87% by Q4 as rate cuts took effect. Portfolio maintained 4.75 days average duration for liquidity, outperforming 3-month SONIA benchmark (4.13%) despite shortened timeframe.
findings.matters: Shows effective cash management during monetary easing cycle; demonstrates ability to balance yield capture against liquidity and security requirements; peer councils benchmark treasury performance against these outcomes.
findings.figures: 4.10% outturn return exactly matching 4.10% budget; £35.587m average investment balance; 4.75 days average duration
findings.quote: In terms of actual performance, the council achieved an outturn investment return of exactly 4.10% for the year, hitting the initial budget target precisely.

findings.headline: Temporary (short-term) borrowing increased £47.5m to £112.5m as council offset Q1 debt repayment and managed Q4 market tightening
findings.detail: Short-term borrowing rose from £65m to £112.5m (£102.5m fixed-rate and £10m variable-rate). Increase reflects both Q1 maturity management and tactical Q4 response to liquidity shortage when long-term rates were unfavorable (5.70%+ for 10-year PWLB).
findings.matters: Shows increased reliance on short-term markets during rate-rise environment; demonstrates council had credit access from banking sector (73% increase evidences market appetite); signals conscious choice of cheaper temporary funding over expensive long-term debt.
findings.figures: Temporary borrowing £112.5m vs £65m opening (£47.5m increase, 73% rise)
findings.quote: temporary borrowing increased by £47.500m, rising from £65m to £112.500m (comprising £102.500m short-term fixed and £10.000m short-term variable market loans)

findings.headline: Council accessed £30m two-year PWLB HRA loan at 4.050% (February 2026) and £35m GLA short-term facility at 5.60% (March 2026) to manage Q4 liquidity stress as inter-authority lending market froze
findings.detail: In late Q4, as 10-year gilt yields spiked to 5.00% and inter-authority lending rates reached 8–9.5%, council secured £30m two-year PWLB loan to 17 June 2028 at 4.050%, then £35m bridge facility from London Treasury Liquidity Fund (Greater London Authority) at 5.60% for 66 days. Tactics avoided entering long-term PWLB market at peak rates.
findings.matters: Demonstrates credit access during acute market stress when primary lending channels freeze; lenders assess whether councils can fund operations when local-to-local authority market seizes; shows reliance on alternative institutional sources.
findings.figures: £30m at 4.050% for 24 months; £35m at 5.60% for ~66 days; inter-authority rates spiked to 8.00–9.50% by late March
findings.quote: the inter-authority lending market experienced an abrupt liquidity shortage, driving short-term local authority rates to historic highs of 8.00% to 9.50% by the end of March 2026
